title: The Great Journey
tagline: He traveled 75,000 miles and wrote the medieval world's greatest travelogue.

scenes.text: Tangier, 1325. Ibn Battuta, 21 years old, sets off for Mecca. He will not return home for 29 years — and he will travel 75,000 miles, more than any person before him.
After the Hajj he keeps going — Egypt, Syria, Persia, East Africa. Every city he reaches offers a new sultan, a new language, a new wonder. He is welcomed as a scholar everywhere.

challenge.instruction: Through Syria and Persia he rides with the caravans, resting at caravanserais a day’s march apart. Buy inns along the road and outtrade the rival merchants before the season ends.
challenge.fact: Ibn Battuta (1304–1368) traveled an estimated 75,000 miles — three times the distance of Marco Polo's journey — visiting the equivalent of 44 modern countries. He crossed the Sahara, sailed the Indian Ocean, traversed the steppes of Central Asia, visited China, and explored the Kingdom of Mali, all within a single lifetime of restless curiosity.

scenes.text: He crosses the Black Death in Central Asia, survives storms at sea, and serves as a judge (qadi) in the Maldives and Mali. He collects four wives and countless stories.

challenge.instruction: Years later he crosses the Sahara to the Mali Empire. Lead the salt caravan south, well to well; each well can be drunk dry only once.
challenge.fact: Ibn Battuta left Tangier in 1325 intending only to make the hajj to Mecca. He was 21 years old. The journey expanded as his curiosity grew — he kept finding reasons not to return home, following trade routes, accepting appointments, and exploring rumors of distant courts. He finally returned to Morocco 29 years later and immediately began planning further travels.

scenes.text: India: he serves the Sultan of Delhi for 8 years, nearly killed multiple times by politics and disaster. Yet he survives to write about it all.

challenge.instruction: The Sultan of Delhi names him envoy to the emperor of China. At Calicut, stow the Sultan’s gifts aboard the junk so she rides level.
challenge.fact: Ibn Battuta's Rihla (A Gift to Those Who Contemplate the Wonders of Cities) was dictated to a court secretary, Ibn Juzayy, on his return. Some scholars have questioned whether he visited every place he describes — the China account in particular is suspiciously vague — but his eyewitness descriptions of Mali, India, and Constantinople remain invaluable historical documents.

scenes.text: China, Southeast Asia, the Golden Horde — he witnesses the Mongol world at its height and its collapse. He meets sultans who remember Genghis's sons.

challenge.instruction: From Constantinople to China, the Mongol peace keeps the roads open. Carry what each city wants and turn a profit along the route.
challenge.fact: The Silk Road was not a single road but a network of shifting routes connecting China to the Mediterranean. Ibn Battuta traveled it in both directions, recording the hospitality of Mongol khans, the luxury of Persian court life, and the stunning efficiency of the Pax Mongolica — the peace imposed by Mongol dominance that made the entire route safe for travelers for the first time.

scenes.text: Back in Morocco, he dictates the Rihla to a scribe — a book that maps the medieval Islamic world more completely than any other document of its age.

challenge.instruction: Dictating in Morocco, he remembers the Swahili coast, where he landed at Mombasa and Kilwa in 1331. Play bao against the Zanzibar master and capture the most seeds.
challenge.fact: Ibn Battuta sailed down the Swahili coast in 1331, stopping at Mombasa and Kilwa. He called Kilwa one of the most beautiful and best-built towns in the world, and praised its sultan, known as “the father of gifts” for his generosity.

challenge.instruction: In Fez the scholar Ibn Juzayy writes the travels down and gives the book its title. Decode the words letter by letter.
challenge.fact: The Arabic language was Ibn Battuta's greatest asset. Across the vast arc from Morocco to China, he could walk into any mosque and find educated men who shared his language, his faith, and his legal tradition. The Islamic world of the 14th century was in many ways more unified than any political empire — held together by shared scripture, shared law, and shared script.

scenes.speaker: Ibn Battuta
scenes.text: Bi Sheng waits at Changan, but nothing is happening there, and without an event there is no fight. I will go first; the turn after I arrive, play the Art Critique card on Changan and we attack.

challenge.instruction: Fight lesson 3 · Starting an Event. Deploy Ibn Battuta to Changan and End Turn. Next turn play the Art Critique card there, add your follower and win one attack.
challenge.fact: Event cards start a scenario at a location where you already have a Great Person, and only one who arrived on an earlier turn can start it. A local event keeps running until a player ends it.
